displayQuote: Peace comes from within. Do not seek it without

meta.title: Who really said "Peace comes from within. Do not seek it without"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — the Buddha never said “Peace comes from within. Do not seek it without.” It’s a 19th-century Western maxim, once credited to Marcus Aurelius, pinned to Buddha only in 1959.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Peace comes from within. Do not seek it without'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the Buddha. It's a reworked Western aphorism — once called 'the message of Marcus Aurelius' — first attributed to Buddha in a 1959 anthology of maxims.

answer.label: Not Buddha — a recycled Western maxim
answer.authorDates: no single author · the wording took shape in Western moral and Christian writing across the 1800s, and was first pinned on the Buddha only in 1959
answer.sourceLine: The line appears nowhere in the Buddhist canon. It is a distillation of a Western “peace within, not without” commonplace that circulated in 19th-century Christian and Stoic writing — a 1908 magazine even called it “the message of Marcus Aurelius” — and it was only attached to the Buddha in the mid-20th century, in G. F. Allen’s 1959 anthology of maxims “attributed to Gotama Buddha.”

source.excerpt: Peace comes from within. Do not seek it without.
trail: Researcher Bodhipaksa traces the earliest English forms to Christian and Stoic writing — e.g. an 1874 devotional and an 1890 “it comes from within” — on Fake Buddha Quotes ↗.
A 1908 issue of Country Life printed the saying and called it “the message of Marcus Aurelius,” per the same chronology ↗.
The earliest known attribution to the Buddha is G. F. Allen’s 1959 “Buddha’s Words of Wisdom” ↗, a book of “maxims and utterances attributed to Gotama Buddha.”
Buddhist practitioners on the Dhamma Wheel forum ↗ agree it is a modern paraphrase with no canonical source, though it echoes genuine teachings like Dhammapada 160.
source.cutTag: ↑ older Western forms, decades before any Buddha attribution
source.excerptNote: This crisp couplet has no canonical original. Its ancestors run through 19th-century Western prose: an 1874 devotional noting people “seek peace of mind…from without, whereas it comes from within,” and by 1890 the reversed form “Peace does not come from without; it comes from within.” A 1908 issue of Country Life printed “Peace comes from within, not from without” and called it “the message of Marcus Aurelius” — not the Buddha.

source.rightsNote: The wording is a short, anonymous aphorism whose components predate 1929, so no live copyright attaches. But it is not a saying of the Buddha — treat “— Buddha” credits as folklore, not attribution.

author.name: G. F. Allen
author.heading: The compiler who first credited it to Buddha
author.bio: George Francis Allen compiled “Buddha’s Words of Wisdom: The Buddhists’ Companion Book” (London: George Allen & Unwin, 1959), a daybook of “365 Maxims and Utterances Attributed to Gotama Buddha.” It is the earliest known source to place “Peace comes from within” in the Buddha’s mouth. As his own subtitle admits, the sayings are “attributed to” the Buddha — a caveat later reposters dropped, hardening a loose attribution into a firm one.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly pinned on
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the most-shared “Buddha” quotes online, yet the Buddha attribution is the youngest layer of its history.

items.why: The exact wording appears in no Buddhist scripture. It is absent from the Pali Canon and, as Bodhipaksa documents, surfaces in English only through 19th-century Western writing before any Buddhist context — the earliest Buddha attribution being a 1959 anthology, per Fake Buddha Quotes ↗. Quote sites nonetheless label it “— Siddhārtha Gautama,” as on Goodreads ↗.

A 1908 issue of Country Life printed “Peace comes from within, not from without” and described it as “the message of Marcus Aurelius” — an attribution that also lacks a source in his Meditations, per the chronology ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no original author to name: the phrase is a Western moral commonplace that hardened into a maxim around 1900 and was only later dressed in Buddhist robes — see the evidence assembled by Fake Buddha Quotes ↗.

context.heading: Why the Buddha label stuck
lead: The sentiment — that lasting peace is found by looking inward rather than to circumstances — genuinely rhymes with Buddhist teaching, which is exactly why the misattribution is so durable. The Buddha did teach self-reliance in verses like Dhammapada 160 (“Oneself, indeed, is one’s own refuge”), so a plausible-sounding maxim slides easily under his name.

But “sounds like something the Buddha would say” is not evidence that he said it. The documented paper trail runs the other way: through Victorian devotional prose and a Stoic-flavored magazine aphorism, reaching the Buddha’s name only in the late 1950s.
context.pull: It sounds like the Buddha — which is precisely why it isn’t traceable to him.
